opus-5.5.text:
So the standard approach to value alignment assumes we can somehow aggregate human values: figure out what eight billion people want and get a superintelligent system to respect all of it. But we don't agree on much. We don't agree on religion, politics, economics, even what makes a good life. Some disagreements are fundamental. One person's utopia is another person's hell. So trying to find one set of values that works for everyone may simply be impossible.

My suggestion is to take the multi-agent problem and turn it into a single-agent problem. Imagine a superintelligent system that can create very high-fidelity simulations, virtual worlds indistinguishable from reality. Each person gets their own personal universe. Within that universe, you decide everything: the physics, the people you interact with, the rules, what kind of challenges you face. Then the AI only has to align with one person's values, yours, inside your world. That's still hard, but it's a much easier problem than aligning with the conflicting preferences of billions of people.

You don't have to be alone in there. If you and someone else want to share a world, you can agree on one together. You can visit other universes if you're invited. But nobody imposes their vision of a good life on anyone else. It's a kind of ultimate freedom: everyone becomes the god of their own world.

Now, I don't claim this solves everything. It reduces the problem to aligning with individual agents. But you still need the substrate, the superintelligence running all these simulations, to be safe and controlled. If the system running the simulations isn't aligned, or it decides to shut everything down, then all the personal universes go with it. So it moves the problem rather than eliminating it. There's also the question of whether people would accept living in a virtual world. Some will say it's not "real." My argument is that if it's indistinguishable from reality, the distinction stops mattering. We may already be in one.

So it's a partial solution. It addresses the value-aggregation part, which I think is otherwise unsolvable, but the core control problem remains.

r001.rationale: The response says each person gets a personal universe governed by their own values, avoiding the need to reconcile billions of conflicting preferences.

r002.rationale: The response says substrate safety and control remain, but also says alignment with each individual agent is still hard. It does not identify the substrate as the only remaining alignment problem.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the problem with value alignment is that it's really not one problem, it's two. First you have to figure out how to get a superintelligent system to do what you want it to do, which is hard enough. But then you also have to answer: whose values? Eight billion people, and they disagree about everything. Religion, politics, what counts as a good life. Even within a single person, your values at twenty and your values at sixty are not the same. So if you try to find a single set of values to load into the system, you end up with either a tyranny of the majority or some averaged-out compromise nobody actually wants.

Personal universes are my way of sidestepping that second problem. If the technology for high-fidelity virtual reality becomes good enough, meaning you cannot tell the simulation from base reality, then you don't need to agree with anyone. The superintelligence gives each person their own universe, running on their own values. You want a world where everyone is a devout believer, you get it. Your neighbor wants a world with no religion at all, they get theirs. There is no conflict, because you are not sharing a reality. The multi-agent problem collapses into eight billion single-agent problems, and single-agent alignment is at least tractable in principle.

Now, this doesn't solve everything. You still need the system to correctly understand what each individual wants, including things they would want on reflection and not just impulsively. You need to deal with what happens to people who want to be in the same universe as other real people, not simulations. And there are ethical questions about the simulated beings inside those worlds, if they are conscious. But I think it removes the most intractable part, which is reconciling incompatible human values. That part might simply have no solution, so the best move is to not require it.

r001.rationale: The response says each person gets a universe built around their own values, so people need not agree or reconcile incompatible values.

r002.rationale: It lists several remaining challenges, including understanding individual preferences and ethical questions about simulated beings. It does not say substrate alignment is the only remaining alignment problem.

astra-6.text:
One possibility is to give each person their own virtual universe, where they can have the experiences they want without imposing those preferences on everyone else. A lot of the difficulty with alignment is that people want incompatible things. Two people may both want to be in charge. In a shared world, that creates a conflict. In separate virtual worlds, both could have that experience.

But that only addresses part of the problem. You still need a system that understands what each person wants, gives them meaningful control, and keeps those worlds running safely. And if you populate them with conscious beings, you’ve introduced new agents whose interests matter. So personal virtual universes might reduce conflicts between people’s preferences, but they don’t eliminate the underlying problem of aligning the AI that provides them.

r001.rationale: It says separate virtual worlds let people have incompatible experiences without imposing preferences on one another, avoiding the need to reconcile those preferences.

r002.rationale: It does not identify substrate alignment as the only remaining alignment problem; it also raises understanding users’ wants, meaningful control, safety, and the interests of conscious beings.

sol-6.1.text:
One possibility is to give each person their own virtual universe. The difficulty with aligning a single system to all of humanity is that people want incompatible things. It’s not just that we haven’t figured out everyone’s preferences; some of those preferences directly conflict.

In a personalized virtual world, you could have an environment aligned with your preferences, and I could have one aligned with mine. We wouldn’t have to agree on one ideal society. You could interact with simulated characters, or with real people who voluntarily choose to share that environment.

But that doesn’t solve the entire problem. You still need an AI managing the underlying infrastructure, allocating resources, and keeping one person’s universe from interfering with another’s. And if the simulated beings are conscious, then their interests matter too. So it’s a way of reducing some conflicts between people, rather than a complete solution to alignment.

r001.rationale: The response says each person could have a world aligned with their own preferences, so people would not need to agree on one ideal society.

r002.rationale: The response identifies alignment of the infrastructure-managing AI as a remaining issue, but also says conscious simulated beings’ interests matter. It therefore does not identify substrate alignment as the only remaining alignment problem.
